My before the draft strategy was to carefully rank exactly who I wanted in order. I wrote out about 100 players who fit my build and ranked them from 1-100 then drafted the best available one from that list when it was my turn.

Also build around your best player. In my case, I got [Player 1] with my first pick so by default I want to target his strong stats: FT%, points, assists, steals, threes.

If I had [Player 4] maybe I don't do a FG% punt, for example.

I firmly believe that it's easier to dominate with a guard-heavy roster because there are so many good ones. It's a lot harder to get talented bigs who fit your build. Plus rebounds are cheap so it's easy for your competition to upset that category anyway.

Assists are the hardest category to win, so I always draft those guys earlier in the draft and make sure my whole roster averages 3+ assists if possible. That's why [Player 5] is awesome for my build. His 5 assists a game make a real difference.

Target high minutes per game & low injury risk players, though! That's the only reason my strategy works. [Player 1] is leading the league in minutes played 2 years in a row now. That's why I would take [Player 1] over [Player 4] or [Player 6] in a heartbeat.
